note_tweet.text:
Starbase This Week (2026-11-22) | Written by @KangasSpaceroo
Wow, what a week it has been. Flight 15 was only a week ago, and SpaceX is showing no signs of slowing down. Of course they had to celebrate catching a Starship for the first time, but this week we’re back to business. Welcome to this week’s Starbase This Week.

Flight 15
Okay okay, Flight 15 was a week and a bit ago now but we can’t stop talking about how historic catching Ship 42 was for the program. While some of us after looking at the heatshield after the catch may have hoped for Ship 42 to refly, Elon gave us an answer on what Ship 42’s fate could be. In an interview on the 18th, he said that Ship 42 might be displayed.

However, he did mention that Ship 42 could be reflown if SpaceX wanted to. In the same interview he mentioned the heat shield looked great. He mentioned that teams would only need a couple weeks of refurbishment, likely due to the tile missing on the body which caused the streak of rust on the heatshield and the roughing up of the ablative sides from the chopsticks. Additionally, he mentioned that the engines looked great as well.

As for displaying vehicles, this is not uncommon with “First” vehicles for SpaceX. Falcon 9 booster B1019, which flew Orbcomm OG-2 in December 2015, was retired and is on display at SpaceX’s Hawthorne factory after demonstrating an orbital class booster landing for the first time. In the Starship program, Booster 12, which flew on Flight 5 back in October 2024, was retired after its historic booster catch. Ship 42 will be in good company in the Rocket Garden if it joins Booster 12 and Ship 20 following post-flight inspections and removal of its Raptors.

Production Site
Now back to business, the booster presumed to fly on Flight 18 continued stacking and the ship presumed for Flight 19 began stacking operations.

In Megabay 1, Booster 25’s transfer tube and AX:2 were stacked this week. The transfer tube is a Falcon 9 first stage sized tube which flows liquid methane from the methane tank and the AX:2 completes the tank and holds the thrust structure for the 33 Raptor 3s powering booster during flight. Over the next couple of weeks we should see its forward section roll in and be stacked ahead of a cryogenic proof test campaign likely in January 2027.

Over in Megabay 2, Ship 46 would begin its construction with the N:3 section rolling on the 19th, followed by the FX:4 section rolling the next day. Based on previous ships, we should expect to see Ship 46 being completed around mid-December.

Before we leave the production site, Gigabay continues through its final stages before full scale production can occur within it. On the 19th the last remaining tower crane was taken apart and is being dismantled as Gigabay has reached full height and major construction of the roof has completed. On the ground, one of Gigabay’s road facing doors was installed on the 20th. Our days of being able to see straight through Gigabay are limited.

Lastly, at the production site, the ship and booster cryostands rolled back from Masseys ahead of Flight 17’s cryogenic proof campaign.

Masseys
Speaking of Flight 17, Ship 44 and Booster 24 both rolled out to Masseys this week ahead of cryogenic proof testing. Both vehicles are currently set to fly on Flight 17 which is likely to occur sometime in Q1 of 2027.

Ship 44 was the first one to roll to Masseys, rolling out during the day on the 19th. Booster 24 followed that evening, arriving early on the 20th.

This week, Ship 44 has been the more active of the two, performing two cryogenic proof tests on the 20th. Additionally, it performed a flap wiggle test while waiting for the first cryogenic proof test. Ship 44 next will roll back to the production site ahead of its static fire campaign, likely to occur in about a month and a half or so.

As for Booster 24, no visible testing occurred this week.

Launch Site
Over at the launch site, an area we don’t talk a whole lot about anymore as its mostly wrapped up in flights. However, this week we have some stuff to talk about!

At Pad 2, following Ship 42’s safing, lowering, and rollback, the dancefloor was lowered into the OLM as teams now move into preparing the pad for Booster 23. While not likely to occur this next week as the US enters Thanksgiving week, we should see Booster 23 roll to the pad sometime in early December ahead of a static fire. Depending on where Ship 43 is in its own static fire and pre-flight preparations, we could see a fifth Starship flight before the year is out.

Over at Pad 1, construction on its flame trench continues with two major wall sections being lifted this week. It hopefully isn’t too much longer before we see two operational pads at Starbase. Potentially, we may even see two full stacks at the same time, similar to seeing two stacks out at LC-39A during the shuttle days.

Well that’s all for this week. Flight 15 was a resounding success but SpaceX doesn’t look to be slowing down at all. When do you think we’ll see Booster 23 and Ship 43 conduct their static fire tests?

For real-time updates, join us in the Discord: https://t.co/hgUICqZQoK

To explore our maps yourself and track every movement, check out our Figma, now at both Starbase and Cape Canaveral:

Starbase: https://t.co/Yuwq34mXNQ

Cape Canaveral: https://t.co/DW4ww1doVg
